title: Two-hour sets and the side door at Child's
summary: The manager demands quiet, calorie-minded early sets, and then the Columbia students pack the room after ten. Nobody noticed that the kids were slipping out the side door without paying.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: it. We called it the Art Hodes Columbia Quintet, featuring Rod Cless Ron Cless and George Brunis and we also -- the three of us split the money. So the three leaders were getting $42.50 apiece and the two side men, $35. It was a big deal.

Now, we came to work, they had all sorts of business there during the daytime. And the manager said to him -- told us, says, now, I don't care what you do at 9:00, or 10:00 when you start playing. And he was very explicit. He says, you can even shit on the floor, if it'll do business. But you play a set from 7:00 to 9:00.

Two hour set. Not continuous. We have people that come in here who have come here for years. We weigh out their food, and he pointed to this little white scale, for calories. And we don't want them disturbed. So whatever you do has to be nice and easy for them.

Now, if you can imagine George Brunis operating the lights. He hasn't had a drink yet that night, playing the chachas with the sticks or with the maracas, whatever it is, and Ron Cless doing the same, and everybody is waiting for that first drink which will happen at 10:00. We're making this scene very sober, right on the ground, and playing the waltzes, changing the lights so that the blue light comes in and the red light and the globe goes around and everything. So that we don't drive these people out.

But meanwhile, none of the None of them are coming in. None. None of them are coming in. They're waiting for 10:00 to come in. At 10:00, -- 9:00 we're through, we got one hour, we got lockers downstairs. Well, by that time, that's lunchtime, if you know what I mean. Everybody has got his own little taste in his own locker, and we're all ready. And you go down there and you get all ready and you relax and you forget about those two hours you just had.

And you're ready. And you come up there and you hit Muskrat or whatever you want to play, and the house is full. Because Gleason and Williams, because they'd been to Columbia and knew that scene, got me a tremendous writeup in the magazine there, and we had all those college kids coming in. Columbia was next door -- to hear this. And what the management did not know was -- or didn't seem to know, although it was their place, was that although they come in through the front door, there was no trick at all for them to go out through the side door, which was not monitored.

Yes. So you're packing the place, -- and we don't know that he's not making it, because all we can see is how good we're doing. Wow, look at the people. They don't see the register. And so the job only lasted ten weeks. Again I'm getting ahead of myself.
